Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Congress passed a $300 billion farm bill over President Bush's veto for a second time Wednesday, a step made necessary by a clerical error when the original bill passed. Congress overrode President Bush's second veto of a $300 billion farm bill. The Senate voted 80-14 to approve the measure over Bush's objections, following a 317-109 vote in the House of Representatives. Both votes were well above the two-thirds majority needed to override the veto, which Bush delivered Wednesday morning. Congress overrode an earlier veto of the farm bill last month, even though lawmakers had discovered that 34 pages were missing in the version originally sent to the White House. In spiking the latest version, Bush said he objected to its continued subsidies for the wealthy and its use of budget gimmicks to hide a $20 billion increase in spending. But Sen. Kent Conrad, the chairman of the Senate Budget Committee, said the measure actually saves the government $110 million. "This bill does not add to the deficit or debt, because this bill is paid for," he said. "That is not my claim. That is the finding of the Congressional Budget Office." The discovery of the missing section, Title III, prompted concerns from House Republicans that the override vote was improper. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi said the sections of the bill that were originally sent to the president had become law after Congress voted to override Bush's first veto. But to put Title III into effect, Congress re-passed the entire legislation, including the missing pages, and resent it to Bush. The House voted 306-110 at the end of May. The Senate voted 77-15 for the bill at the beginning of June. Two-thirds of the $300 billion in spending for the farm bill will go for nutrition programs such as food stamps. Another $40 billion will go toward farm subsidies, and $30 billion is allocated for payments to farms to keep land idle and other environmental programs. After vetoing the latest version of the farm bill, Bush scolded Congress on Wednesday for not "modifying certain objectionable, onerous and fiscally imprudent provisions. ... I am returning this bill for the same reasons as stated in my veto message." When he vetoed the first version of the farm bill, Bush said it "continues subsidies for the wealthy and increases farm bill spending by more than $20 billion, while using budget gimmicks to hide much of the increase." The president said it would hurt efforts to improve American farmers' access to overseas markets. Congress has passed one other bill over Bush's objections: legislation for a $23 billion water project that the president vetoed in 2007. CNN Capitol Hill producer Deirdre Walsh contributed to this report.

The House approved the bill 306–110 at the end of May, and the Senate passed it 77–15 at the beginning of June.

When he vetoed the first version, Bush said the bill “continues subsidies for the wealthy and increases farm bill spending by more than $20 billion, while using budget gimmicks to hide much of the increase.”

WASHINGTON (CNN) — On Wednesday, Congress again overrode President Bush’s veto of a $300 billion farm bill, repeating the process because a clerical mistake had affected the legislation’s original passage.

The Senate voted 80-14 to enact the measure despite Bush’s opposition, after the House approved the override by 317-109. Both chambers exceeded the two-thirds majority required to overturn the veto, which the president issued Wednesday morning.

Lawmakers had already overridden Bush’s first veto of the bill the previous month. However, they later learned that the version initially delivered to the White House was missing 34 pages.

Bush rejected the corrected legislation because, he said, it maintained subsidies for affluent recipients and relied on accounting maneuvers to conceal a $20 billion spending increase.

Sen. Kent Conrad, who chaired the Senate Budget Committee, disputed that assessment, saying the bill would save the federal government $110 million. He emphasized that the measure was fully funded and therefore would not increase either the national debt or the budget deficit, adding that this was the conclusion of the Congressional Budget Office rather than merely his own assertion.

The omitted portion, known as Title III, led House Republicans to question whether the first veto override had been valid. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi maintained that the provisions originally submitted to the president became law when Congress overturned Bush’s initial veto.

To ensure that Title III also took effect, lawmakers passed the complete bill again, this time including the missing material, and returned it to Bush. The House approved the corrected measure 306-110 in late May, while the Senate passed it 77-15 in early June.

Approximately two-thirds of the bill’s $300 billion in spending was designated for nutrition assistance, including food stamps. Another $40 billion was set aside for agricultural subsidies, while $30 billion was allocated to environmental initiatives and payments to farmers who leave land unused.

After vetoing the revised bill, Bush criticized Congress on Wednesday for failing to change provisions he considered objectionable, burdensome and financially irresponsible. He said he was sending the legislation back for the same reasons outlined in his first veto statement.

When rejecting the earlier version, Bush argued that the legislation preserved subsidies for wealthy beneficiaries, raised farm-bill spending by more than $20 billion and used budgetary devices to obscure much of that increase. He also said the measure would undermine attempts to expand American farmers’ access to foreign markets.

This was only the second time Congress had enacted legislation over Bush’s veto. The other instance involved a $23 billion water-project bill that Bush rejected in 2007.

CNN Capitol Hill producer Deirdre Walsh contributed to the report.

The votes completed enactment of the five-year measure and resolved the procedural problem created by the missing pages.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news report about Congress overriding President George W. Bush’s veto of the $300 billion farm bill for a second time after a clerical error omitted 34 pages.
counterfactuals.output:
# Congress overrides Bush veto of farm bill — again

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — Congress has overridden President George W. Bush’s veto of a roughly $300 billion farm bill for the second time, after a clerical error forced lawmakers to repeat the process.

The House voted 317-109 Wednesday to override the president’s veto, followed by an 80-14 Senate vote. Both margins exceeded the two-thirds majority required by the Constitution.

Congress initially approved the five-year legislation in May and quickly overrode Bush’s first veto. But officials later discovered that 34 pages — an entire section dealing with international food aid and trade — had been omitted from the version sent to the White House.

Because the president had vetoed an incomplete copy, lawmakers passed the full bill again and sent it back to Bush. He vetoed the measure a second time, citing its cost and continued subsidies for some wealthy farmers.

The legislation expands nutrition programs, supports conservation efforts and maintains subsidies for major crops. Supporters said it provides an important safety net for farmers and low-income families at a time of rising food prices.

Bush argued that the bill was too expensive and failed to make sufficient reforms to farm-payment programs.

With the second override, the complete legislation becomes law, bringing an unusual end to a legislative dispute complicated by a paperwork mistake.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the June 2008 congressional votes to override Bush’s farm bill veto, including the House and Senate vote totals, the missing Title III controversy, and the bill’s major spending provisions.
counterfactuals.output:
In June 2008, Congress overrode President George W. Bush’s second veto of the 2008 farm bill:

- **House:** **317–109** on June 18  
- **Senate:** **80–14** later that day  

Both exceeded the two-thirds majority required.

### Missing Title III controversy
The unusual second vote resulted from a clerical error in the first version sent to the White House. The enrolled bill accidentally omitted **Title III—34 pages covering agricultural trade and international food-aid programs**. Bush vetoed that incomplete version in May, and Congress overrode him, but the omission raised constitutional questions because the text approved by Congress was not identical to the text presented to the president.

To eliminate any doubt, Congress passed the full bill again as **H.R. 6124**, including Title III. Bush vetoed it again, arguing that it was too costly and did too little to reform subsidies, prompting the June overrides.

### Major spending provisions
The five-year law was commonly estimated at roughly **$290 billion**—with totals varying somewhat by budget baseline—and included:

- About **two-thirds for nutrition programs**, especially food stamps, later renamed **SNAP**
- Continued commodity-price supports and direct payments to farmers
- Expanded conservation programs
- Crop-insurance subsidies and a permanent agricultural disaster-assistance program
- Funding for rural development, agricultural research, renewable energy, and specialty-crop programs
- Increased support for fruit-and-vegetable purchases and school nutrition initiatives

The bill became law over Bush’s veto as the **Food, Conservation, and Energy Act of 2008**.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed news article explaining why Congress had to pass and override a veto of the same farm bill twice, along with Bush’s objections and lawmakers’ response.
counterfactuals.output:
# Congress Overrode Bush Twice on One Farm Bill Because of a Printing Error

**WASHINGTON —** Congress’s extraordinary decision in 2008 to pass the same sweeping farm bill twice—and to override President George W. Bush’s veto twice—was not the result of a constitutional dispute or a change in policy. It was caused by a clerical error that left an entire section of the legislation out of the official copy sent to the White House.

The episode turned an already contentious debate over agricultural subsidies, nutrition assistance and federal spending into a rare legislative do-over. Although lawmakers had approved a complete bill, the version formally “enrolled” and presented to Bush was missing the 34-page trade title. Congress overrode the president’s first veto before the full implications of the mistake were resolved, leaving most—but not all—of the farm bill in law.

To enact the measure exactly as Congress had intended, lawmakers had to approve the complete text again, send it to Bush again and, after he rejected it again, muster the required two-thirds majorities for a second set of overrides.

## A major bill with broad bipartisan support

The legislation, known as the Food, Conservation, and Energy Act of 2008, was the product of lengthy negotiations between the House and Senate. It renewed federal farm policy for five years and covered far more than traditional crop subsidies.

Among its major provisions were:

- Commodity-support and crop-insurance programs;
- Nutrition assistance, including food-stamp benefits;
- Conservation incentives for farmers and landowners;
- Rural development initiatives;
- Agricultural research;
- Renewable-energy and biofuel programs;
- International food aid and agricultural trade programs; and
- A permanent disaster-assistance fund for farmers.

The bill carried a projected five-year cost of roughly $300 billion, although most of that money was associated with nutrition programs rather than direct payments to farmers.

Its coalition was unusually broad. Farm-state Republicans supported crop and disaster programs, while Democrats emphasized increased nutrition assistance, conservation and rural development. That combination produced veto-proof margins despite opposition from the Bush administration.

In May 2008, the House approved the final conference agreement 318-106, and the Senate passed it 81-15.

## Bush’s objections

Bush argued that the bill spent too much and did too little to reform the system of federal farm subsidies.

The administration had called for stricter limits on payments to wealthy farmers and landowners. White House officials contended that the congressional bill still allowed people with very high incomes—potentially as much as $1.5 million under some eligibility calculations—to receive federal agricultural benefits.

Bush also objected to new and continued subsidies at a time when commodity prices and farm incomes were relatively strong. The administration said Congress had missed an opportunity to make farm policy more market-oriented and to reduce government support for producers who did not need it.

Other White House concerns included:

- The overall cost of the legislation;
- The creation of new subsidy and disaster programs;
- Tax and revenue provisions used to finance parts of the bill;
- The possibility that some crop supports could complicate U.S. obligations in international trade negotiations;
- Benefits directed toward particular crops or regions; and
- What the administration characterized as insufficient reform of payment limits and farm-program eligibility.

Bush said the measure expanded government and continued an outdated subsidy structure rather than concentrating aid on farmers with genuine financial need. He vetoed the bill on May 21, 2008.

## Congress’s response

Lawmakers from both parties rejected the administration’s criticism and argued that the bill represented a carefully balanced compromise.

Supporters said the legislation did make reforms, including tightening some income and payment restrictions, while preserving a safety net for farmers facing volatile weather, fuel and fertilizer costs, and unstable markets. They also noted that the bill’s largest component was nutrition assistance, not farm subsidies.

Democratic leaders stressed that the measure increased support for low-income families at a time of rising food prices. Farm-state lawmakers emphasized disaster relief, conservation, rural infrastructure and long-term stability for producers. Supporters also argued that many of the bill’s new costs were offset by spending reductions or additional revenue elsewhere in the legislation.

The breadth of the coalition made the veto ineffective. On May 21, the House voted 316-108 to override Bush. The Senate followed on May 22 by a vote of 82-13, comfortably exceeding the constitutional requirement of a two-thirds majority in each chamber.

Ordinarily, that would have ended the matter.

## The missing title

But the official copy sent to the president was not the same as the measure lawmakers believed they had passed.

During preparation of the enrolled bill—the final parchment copy authenticated by the House and Senate and transmitted to the White House—Title III had been omitted. That title contained provisions dealing with agricultural trade and international food-aid programs.

The omission apparently resulted from a printing or document-assembly error. The section had been included in the conference agreement approved by both chambers, but it disappeared from the official enrolled version.

Under the Constitution, the president acts on the specific bill presented to him. Congress’s first override therefore enacted the incomplete version. Fourteen of the bill’s 15 titles became law as **Public Law 110-234**, but the missing trade title did not.

The error could not simply be corrected by inserting the missing pages after the fact. Once a bill has been presented to the president, vetoed and overridden, its legal text is the text that went through that process. Congressional leaders therefore had to move a complete version through the legislative system again.

## A second passage and a second veto

Congress introduced the full bill again as **H.R. 6124**, including the omitted trade title. Lawmakers treated it as a replacement for the defective version and passed it with another round of large bipartisan majorities.

Bush’s policy position had not changed. Because the new measure contained substantially the same farm, nutrition and subsidy policies he had rejected the first time, he vetoed it on June 18.

Congress then repeated the override process. The House voted 317-109 to override the second veto, and the Senate followed on June 19 by a vote of 80-14.

The complete measure became **Public Law 110-246**. Congress also provided that the earlier, incomplete law would be repealed, preventing two overlapping versions of the farm bill from remaining on the books.

## A rare but legally necessary do-over

The double veto override was highly unusual because Congress was not reconsidering the substance of the bill. Lawmakers had already demonstrated overwhelming support for the policy. The second passage was required to repair a procedural defect in the official text.

The episode highlighted the importance of “enrollment,” a normally routine stage of lawmaking. Before legislation reaches the president, congressional clerks must assemble and verify the final text approved by both chambers. A mistake at that stage can have constitutional consequences because neither Congress nor the White House can informally rewrite a bill after presentation.

In practical terms, the first override enacted an incomplete farm bill. The second enacted the complete bill Congress had intended all along.

The result was a legislative oddity: Bush vetoed essentially the same farm bill twice for the same policy reasons, and Congress overrode him twice with nearly identical bipartisan coalitions—the first time to defeat his objections, and the second time to correct its own clerical mistake.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.output:
**Congress overrides Bush veto to enact $300 billion farm bill**

WASHINGTON — Congress enacted a roughly $300 billion, five-year farm bill over President George W. Bush’s objections, with the House voting **317-109** and the Senate **80-14** to override his veto. Both margins easily exceeded the two-thirds required.

The legislation increases spending on **food stamps and other nutrition programs**, including benefit and eligibility changes intended to help low-income families cope with rising food prices. Nutrition assistance accounts for the largest share of the bill.

It also continues extensive **farm subsidies**, including commodity supports, crop insurance and disaster assistance. Although the measure tightens some eligibility rules, critics said wealthy farmers and landowners would still receive federal payments. Bush argued that Congress missed an opportunity to make farm policy more market-oriented and to direct aid more narrowly to farmers in genuine need.

The bill provides billions of dollars for **environmental and conservation programs**, rewarding farmers for protecting wetlands, reducing soil erosion, improving water quality and preserving working farmland. It also supports renewable energy and rural-development initiatives.

The central dispute was over the budget. The administration contended that the bill cost too much and relied on accounting devices and projected revenue to claim that new spending was offset. Congressional supporters said the package complied with budget rules and balanced nutrition aid, the farm safety net and conservation needs.

The final override also resolved an earlier procedural problem in which a section of the bill was accidentally omitted from the version initially sent to the White House, forcing Congress to pass and present the complete measure again.
